options.why: By default React renders the whole subtree below the component whose state changed.

options.text: It is skipped, because React notices that it takes no props and so cannot be affected
options.why: React does not inspect props unless the component opts in with `React.memo`.

options.text: It re-renders only when its output would differ from the DOM that is already on screen
options.why: Comparing output against the DOM happens after rendering, during commit; the render itself still runs.

options.text: It is unmounted and mounted again so that its state starts fresh on each click
options.why: Same type at the same position keeps the instance. Only a type or key change remounts it.

explanation: When a component re-renders, React calls every child component below it again, whether or not their props changed. Re-rendering is not the same as touching the DOM: if the output is identical, the commit phase makes no DOM changes. Opting out of the render needs `React.memo` (or the React Compiler), or restructuring so the state lives lower in the tree.

stem: `React.memo(Component)` stops the component from re-rendering when its own state changes or when a context it reads with `useContext` changes.

options.text: True
options.why: It only skips renders caused by the parent re-rendering with the same props.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: memo compares props only. State updates and context changes still re-render the component.

explanation: Memoization is about props. A memoized component still re-renders when its own state updates or when the value of a context it reads changes, because those are not props. If a memoized component is re-rendering unexpectedly, check its state and contexts before blaming the parent.

stem: In development, a component is mounted inside `<StrictMode>` with one `useEffect` that has an empty dependency array. Put what React does on that first mount in order.

options.text: Call the component function (render)
options.why: The first render.

options.text: Call the component function a second time and discard one result
options.why: The extra render that surfaces impure rendering.

options.text: Run the effect setup
options.why: The first effect setup after commit.

options.text: Run the effect cleanup
options.why: The simulated unmount.

options.text: Run the effect setup again
options.why: The simulated remount.

explanation: Strict Mode in development renders each component twice and then runs effects through an extra setup → cleanup → setup cycle, to expose impure renders and missing cleanups. Counting with a console.log shows two renders, two setups and one cleanup on mount. None of this happens in a production build, so do not judge performance by the doubled logs.

stem: Which tab in React DevTools records commits and shows how long each component took to render and why it rendered? Type the tab name.
explanation: The Profiler tab records each commit, shows flame and ranked charts of render time, and (with "Record why each component rendered" turned on) the reason for every render: hooks changed, props changed, parent rendered. Use it before reaching for memoization.

stem: A team wants to know whether a page is really slow for users. Which two practices give trustworthy measurements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Profile a production build (with React's profiling build enabled), not the development server
options.why: Development React does extra checks and Strict Mode double renders, so it is much slower than production.

options.text: Throttle the CPU in browser DevTools to approximate the slower devices real users have
options.why: A fast laptop hides problems that a mid-range phone will show.

options.text: Count console.log lines in development, since each log is one render that users will also pay for
options.why: Strict Mode doubles renders in development, so the counts are inflated.

options.text: Trust the dev-mode Profiler timings directly, since dev and prod run the same reconciliation code
options.why: The algorithm is the same, but dev builds add warnings and checks that change the timings a lot.

options.text: Measure once on a cold load and treat that single run as the answer
options.why: Timings vary from run to run; you need several runs and a realistic interaction.

explanation: Development builds of React are deliberately slower (validation, warnings, Strict Mode double rendering), so performance work should be measured on a production build, ideally with the profiling-enabled build so the DevTools Profiler still works. CPU throttling helps approximate real devices. Logs in dev overstate render counts.

stem: Match each tool with what it does.

options.text: React.memo
options.why: Skips a component render when props are shallowly equal.

options.text: useMemo
options.why: Caches a computed value between renders.

options.text: useCallback
options.why: Caches a function identity between renders.

options.text: React.lazy
options.why: Loads a component's code on demand.

prompts.text: Skip re-rendering a component whose props have not changed
Avoid recomputing an expensive filtered list on every render
Keep the same function object between renders so a memoized child can skip
Split a rarely used editor out of the initial JavaScript bundle

explanation: These four tools solve different problems. `memo` skips renders, `useMemo` caches values, `useCallback` caches function identity (it is `useMemo` for functions), and `lazy` defers loading code until it is first rendered. The first three only help when something compares identities; `lazy` helps load time, not render time.

stem: What does wrapping a route component in `React.lazy(() => import('./Settings'))` and rendering it inside `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` do? (Choose two.)

options.text: The Settings code goes into a separate chunk that downloads only when the component first renders
options.why: Dynamic `import()` is the split point bundlers use for code splitting.

options.text: While the chunk is loading, the nearest Suspense boundary shows its fallback
options.why: The lazy component suspends until its module resolves.

options.text: Settings renders faster on every visit because React caches its rendered HTML
options.why: lazy affects loading code, not render speed, and React does not cache rendered output.

options.text: The chunk is downloaded again each time the user navigates back to the route
options.why: Once the module promise resolves, the lazy component reuses it.

options.text: Settings is rendered on the server only, so its code never reaches the browser
options.why: lazy is a client code-splitting tool; it does not make a component server-only.

explanation: React.lazy plus a dynamic import lets the bundler split a component into its own chunk. The first render suspends, the nearest `<Suspense>` shows its fallback, and the component appears when the module loads. Later renders reuse the loaded module. It reduces initial bundle size; it does not speed up rendering.

explanation: React.memo compares each prop with `Object.is`. An inline object literal is a new object on every render, so the comparison fails and Box renders every time Parent does, which makes the memo useless. Hoist the constant object outside the component, or memoize it with `useMemo`. Counting renders confirms one extra render of Box per parent update.

options.why: Looking identical is not enough: memo compares the element objects by reference.

explanation: JSX is just `jsx('span', …)` calls that return fresh objects, so passing JSX as children means the `children` prop is a new object each render and `memo` always fails. If you need Card to skip, memoize the children element (`useMemo(() => Hello, [])`) or restructure. Measured: Card renders once per Page update, and zero times once the children element is memoized.

options.why: A stable function reference passes the shallow comparison.

options.why: Primitives and module-level constants are identical on every render.

options.why: Changing the key remounts the row, which is more work than a re-render.

options.why: Class components compare nothing unless they use PureComponent or shouldComponentUpdate, and that comparison is shallow too.

explanation: For memo to skip, every prop must be identical (`Object.is`) to the previous render. Here `item` is stable (it comes from the `items` prop), but two props are recreated on every render: the inline arrow and the `options` literal. Both must be stabilised before Row can skip, because one unstable prop is enough to fail the comparison.

options.why: memo cannot block a context change; consumers re-render when the value changes.

options.why: Context compares values with Object.is, and a new object literal never matches.

options.why: Sidebar does not read the context, and memo skips it because its props are unchanged.

options.text: Only Sidebar re-renders, because Toolbar receives the same `user` string
options.why: The context value is the wrapper object, not the string inside it.

explanation: React compares the provider `value` with `Object.is`. An inline `{ user }` is a fresh object on every render, so every component that reads that context re-renders, even memoized ones, even though `user` did not change. Components that do not read the context are unaffected. Fix it with `const value = useMemo(() => ({ user }), [user])`. Measured: Toolbar renders once per App update with the inline value and zero times with the memoized value.

`useState(buildIndex())` calls `buildIndex()` on every render, because the argument is evaluated before `useState` is called. React uses the result only on the first render and throws it away afterwards. Mount + 2 updates = 3 calls. Pass the function itself, `useState(buildIndex)`, and React calls it once (twice on mount in Strict Mode development).
reference: react.dev: useState (Avoiding recreating the initial state)

stem: You are diagnosing a slow "add to cart" interaction with the React DevTools Profiler. Put the steps in a sensible order.

options.text: Build the app with profiling enabled in production mode
options.why: Measure realistic code.

options.text: Start recording in the Profiler tab
options.why: Recording must be on before the interaction.

options.text: Perform the slow interaction once
options.why: Capture only the work you care about.

options.text: Stop recording and select the slowest commit
options.why: Find where the time went.

options.text: Check which components rendered in that commit and why
options.why: This tells you what to fix.

explanation: Profile a production-like build, record just the interaction, then look at the slowest commit in the flame or ranked chart and at the "why did this render" reasons. Only then choose a fix: move state down, stabilise props, memoize, or virtualize. Guessing first usually adds memoization where it doesn't matter.

stem: Match each performance problem with the technique that best fixes it.

options.text: Virtualize the list
options.why: Render only the visible rows.

options.text: Code-split with React.lazy
options.why: Load the code on demand.

options.text: Memoize the computation with useMemo
options.why: Skip the recomputation.

options.text: Split one context into several
options.why: Narrow who re-renders.

options.text: Debounce the handler
options.why: Fire once after typing pauses.

prompts.text: A table with 20,000 rows makes scrolling janky
A charting library used on one admin page bloats the initial bundle
Sorting 5,000 items runs on every render, even when the items have not changed
Changing the theme re-renders every component that reads the logged-in user
A search box calls the API on every keystroke

explanation: Each symptom points at a different bottleneck: too many DOM nodes (virtualize), too much JavaScript up front (code split), repeated pure computation (useMemo), over-broad subscriptions (split context), and too many events (debounce). Profile first to confirm which one you have.

options.text: Dashboard and Counter, because a state change re-renders from the root down
options.why: Rendering starts at the component that owns the state, not at the root.

options.text: Only Counter (and anything it renders)
options.why: State updates re-render the owning component and its descendants, never its ancestors.

options.text: Only Dashboard, which then decides whether Counter needs updating
options.why: The parent is not involved in a child's own state update.

options.text: Neither, until the parent passes new props down
options.why: A state update schedules a render of the component that owns the state.

explanation: React starts rendering at the component whose state changed and walks down from there. Parents are not re-rendered by a child's state update. That is the basis of the "move state down" technique: keep fast-changing state in the smallest component that needs it.

stem: Calling `setSettings({ theme: 'dark' })` when the current state is already an object with exactly `{ theme: 'dark' }` skips the re-render, because React deep-compares the new state with the old one.

options.text: True
options.why: React only skips when the new state is identical by Object.is.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a new object is never Object.is-equal to the old one, so the component re-renders.

explanation: React compares the next state with the current one using `Object.is`. A new object with the same contents is a different reference, so React re-renders. Use the functional form and return the previous object when nothing changed, or store primitives, if you want the bail-out.

options.text: 4, one for each state update
options.why: React batches updates instead of rendering after each one.

options.text: 2, one batch before the await and one batch after it
options.why: Updates in the same synchronous run are batched; the code after the await runs in a later task and forms a second batch.

options.text: 1, because React batches every update made in the same event handler, across awaits
options.why: Batching groups updates that happen together; the await splits the handler into two separate runs.

options.text: 3, because updates after an await are never batched in React
options.why: Since React 18, automatic batching also applies inside promises and timeouts.

explanation: React 18+ batches all updates made in the same synchronous run, in event handlers, promises and timeouts alike. The first two updates are one render. After `await`, the remaining code runs later, and its two updates form a second batch. Total: 2 renders. Before React 18, updates after the await were not batched at all.
reference: react.dev: Queueing a Series of State Updates

stem: The `<Profiler>` callback reports both `actualDuration` and `baseDuration` for a commit. What is the difference?

options.text: `actualDuration` is this commit's render time; `baseDuration` estimates the subtree with no memoization
options.why: A big gap between them shows that memoization is saving work.

options.text: `actualDuration` includes the time the browser spent painting; `baseDuration` covers only the React render
options.why: Neither value includes browser paint; both measure React rendering work.

options.text: `actualDuration` is measured in production builds and `baseDuration` in development builds
options.why: Both are reported in the same build, whenever profiling is enabled.

options.text: `baseDuration` is the duration of the first mount, while `actualDuration` is that of the latest update
options.why: baseDuration is recomputed per commit as a worst-case estimate, not frozen at mount.

explanation: `onRender(id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime)`: `actualDuration` is the time spent rendering the Profiler subtree for this commit, which goes down when memoized components skip. `baseDuration` estimates how long rendering the whole subtree would take without any skipping. Comparing the two shows how much memoization helps.

options.why: Where an element appears in the output doesn't matter; what matters is who created it.

options.text: No: App created that element, and App did not re-render
options.why: The children prop is the same element object, so React skips that subtree.

options.text: Yes, unless ExpensiveTree is wrapped in React.memo
options.why: No memo is needed here; the element itself is unchanged.

options.text: No, but only because ExpensiveTree has no props
options.why: It would be skipped with props too, as long as App did not re-render.

explanation: This is the "lift content up" technique. `<ExpensiveTree />` is created in App. When ColorPicker's state changes, only ColorPicker re-renders, and the `children` it renders is the very same element object as before, so React bails out of that subtree without any memo. Measured: one ColorPicker render, zero ExpensiveTree renders.

stem: A product page has a search input whose state lives at the top of a large component, and every keystroke re-renders hundreds of product cards that don't depend on the query. What is the simplest effective fix?

options.text: Wrap every product card in React.memo and every handler in useCallback
options.why: That can work, but it is more code and is easy to break with one unstable prop.

options.text: Move the input and its state into its own small component
options.why: State that only the input needs should live next to the input.

options.text: Store the query in a ref instead of state so typing never causes a render
options.why: Then the input and any results that do depend on the query would stop updating.

options.text: Debounce the input so the page re-renders at most every 300 ms
options.why: That lowers how often the cost hits but keeps the unnecessary renders, and makes the input feel laggy.

explanation: "Move state down": state should live in the lowest component that needs it. Extracting the input into `<SearchBox />` means keystrokes re-render only that component, and the product grid is not touched. Composition fixes like this beat sprinkling memo, because they cannot be undone by an unstable prop somewhere.

options.text: Only when `items` changes, because `options` always has the same contents
options.why: useMemo compares dependencies with Object.is, not by contents.

options.text: On every render, because `options` is a new object each time
options.why: A dependency created during render changes on every render.

options.text: Once, because useMemo caches the first result for the life of the component
options.why: useMemo recomputes whenever a dependency changes.

options.text: Only in development, because useMemo dependencies are compared deeply in production
options.why: The comparison is Object.is in every build.

explanation: Each render creates a new `options` object, so the dependency array always differs and the memo never hits: `expensiveFilter` runs on mount and on every page change. Move the constant object outside the component, list its primitive fields as dependencies, or memoize it. Measured: 3 computations for 3 renders.

options.text: Nothing special: Row re-renders like any child and keeps its state
options.why: A component defined inside another is a new function, and so a new type, on every render.

options.text: Every Row remounts: `open` resets and effects re-subscribe
options.why: React sees a different component type at the same position, so it throws the old subtree away.

options.text: Rows keep their state because they have stable keys, but their effects re-run
options.why: Keys are compared only between elements of the same type, so they can't preserve state here.

options.text: React shows a warning and reuses the first definition of Row
options.why: React gives no such warning; it just treats each new function as a new type.

explanation: Declaring a component inside another creates a brand-new function on every render, and React compares element types by identity. A different type means unmount and mount: state is lost, effects re-run, and the DOM is rebuilt. It is a serious performance and correctness bug. Measured over two Table updates: three mounts and two unmounts per row. Define Row at module level.

stem: An app provides two separate contexts, `ThemeContext` and `UserContext`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A component that reads only ThemeContext does not re-render when only the UserContext value changes
options.why: Each context notifies only its own consumers.

options.text: Every component that reads UserContext re-renders when its value changes, even if it uses only one field of it
options.why: A context has no field-level subscriptions; any value change notifies every consumer.

options.text: Wrapping a UserContext consumer in React.memo stops it re-rendering when the UserContext value changes
options.why: memo compares props; context changes go around it.

options.text: React deep-compares the provider value, so a new object with the same fields notifies no one
options.why: The comparison is Object.is.

options.text: Components between a provider and its consumers re-render whenever the context value changes
options.why: Intermediate components are skipped unless they read the context themselves.

explanation: Context subscriptions are per context and per value: a value change re-renders every consumer of that context (memoized or not), and nothing else. Splitting a broad context into narrower ones is the standard fix for "the whole app re-renders when X changes". For field-level selection, use an external store with `useSyncExternalStore` and a selector. Measured: changing one of two split contexts re-rendered only its consumer.

options.text: Both, because the store notifies every subscriber and both are subscribed
options.why: Being notified is not the same as re-rendering; React compares each snapshot first.

options.text: Only ShowA, because ShowB's snapshot (the primitive `b`) is unchanged by Object.is
options.why: React re-renders a subscriber only when its getSnapshot result changes.

options.text: Neither, because useSyncExternalStore updates are deferred until the next transition
options.why: External store updates are synchronous and cannot be deferred.

options.text: Only ShowB, because ShowA already holds the latest value
options.why: ShowA's snapshot changed from 1 to 2, so it must re-render.

explanation: On each store notification React calls every subscriber's `getSnapshot` and re-renders only those whose result changed by `Object.is`. Selecting a primitive slice therefore gives field-level subscriptions, which is how Zustand and Redux selectors avoid the context problem. The trap: if `getSnapshot` returns a new object or array each call, React sees a change every time and warns about an infinite loop.

stem: A list renders rows with `key={Math.random()}` "to make sure they update". What is the performance impact?

options.text: None, because keys only matter for React's warnings, not for rendering
options.why: Keys decide whether React keeps or recreates each item.

options.text: Rows render slightly more often, but keep their state and DOM nodes
options.why: A new key means a different identity, so state and DOM are not kept.

options.text: Every render unmounts and remounts every row: DOM nodes are rebuilt, state resets and effects re-run
options.why: A key that changes on every render tells React each item is brand new.

options.text: React detects random keys and falls back to using the array index
options.why: React has no such detection; it uses whatever key you give it.

explanation: React matches children between renders by key. A random key never matches, so every row is destroyed and recreated on each render: DOM nodes are rebuilt from scratch, local state and focus are lost, and effects clean up and run again. Measured: changing a key gives one unmount and one fresh mount. Use a stable id from the data.

options.text: The new price, because React ignores a comparator that always returns true
options.why: React trusts the comparator completely.

options.text: The original price, forever
options.why: The comparator returning true tells React the props are equal, so every update from new props is skipped.

options.text: The new price, but only after the next state change inside PriceTag
options.why: PriceTag has no state; and even with state the stale props would remain.

options.text: A React error saying memo comparators must sometimes return false
options.why: React gives no such validation.

explanation: The second argument to `memo` is `arePropsEqual(prev, next)`: returning `true` means skip. A comparator that always returns true freezes the component on its first props. Measured: the component saw only its initial value across two updates. Custom comparators must compare every prop, including functions, or they will cause stale UI bugs that are hard to trace.

stem: When does wrapping a function in `useCallback` actually improve performance? (Choose three.)

options.text: When the function is passed to a child wrapped in React.memo
options.why: A stable reference lets memo's shallow comparison pass.

options.text: When the function is a dependency of a useEffect or useMemo that should not re-run on every render
options.why: An unstable function in a dependency list re-triggers the effect or recomputation.

options.text: When a custom hook returns it and callers use it in their own dependency lists
options.why: Stable identities from hooks spare every caller from re-running work.

options.text: Whenever a function is passed to a native element such as `<button onClick>`
options.why: DOM elements are not memoized, so a new handler costs nothing measurable.

options.text: Always, because creating a function on each render is expensive
options.why: Creating a closure is cheap; useCallback adds its own bookkeeping and dependency checks.

explanation: useCallback only matters when something compares function identity: a memoized child, a dependency array, or a hook consumer. Elsewhere it adds noise and slightly more work. With the React Compiler enabled, this memoization is done automatically, which is why new code rarely needs manual useCallback.

options.text: useDeferredValue works only inside a Suspense boundary
options.why: It works without Suspense; Suspense is only needed for showing stale content while data loads.

options.text: SlowList isn't memoized, so it still renders in the urgent pass
options.why: Without memo, Search re-rendering re-renders SlowList even though its deferred prop is unchanged.

options.text: The input must be uncontrolled for deferred values to take effect
options.why: Controlled inputs are the normal use case in the docs.

options.text: useDeferredValue delays rendering by a fixed 300 ms, which still feels slow
options.why: There is no fixed delay; React renders the deferred value as soon as it can, in the background.

explanation: useDeferredValue makes React first re-render with the old `deferredText`, then render again in the background with the new one. That only helps if the urgent render can skip SlowList, which requires `memo(SlowList)`: its `text` prop is unchanged in the urgent pass. Without memo, SlowList renders in both passes and the input stays slow.

stem: A tab bar switches between heavy tab panels. Which state update should go inside `startTransition` to keep clicks and typing responsive?

options.text: The update that changes which tab panel is shown
options.why: Rendering the new panel is the slow, interruptible part.

options.text: The update that stores the text a user is typing into a controlled input
options.why: Controlled input updates must be urgent, or the input lags and loses characters.

options.text: Every update in the component, so that React can schedule all of them optimally
options.why: Marking urgent updates as transitions makes direct feedback feel slower.

options.text: The update that shows a spinner while the panel loads
options.why: Use the `isPending` flag from useTransition for that instead of a separate update.

explanation: Transitions mark updates as non-urgent and interruptible. Put the expensive navigation (switching the panel) in `startTransition`, and React keeps the old UI interactive while it renders the new one, abandoning stale renders if the user clicks again. Direct feedback such as input values must stay urgent. Use `isPending` for the pending indicator.

stem: If a component logs twice per update in local development, it will also render twice per update for real users in production.

options.text: True
options.why: Double rendering is a development-only Strict Mode check.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Strict Mode's double render runs only in development; production renders once.

explanation: Strict Mode intentionally calls component functions twice in development to surface impure rendering. Production builds render once. That is one reason performance must be measured on production builds: development logs and timings exaggerate the cost.

stem: With the React Compiler enabled, what directive string do you put at the top of one component's function body to opt only that component out of automatic memoization? Type the directive text without quotes.
explanation: The React Compiler lets you opt individual functions out with the `"use no memo"` directive as a temporary escape hatch, typically while you fix code that breaks the Rules of React. The opposite directive, `"use memo"`, opts a function in when the compiler runs in annotation mode.

options.text: useLayoutEffect runs on a background thread, so the measurements arrive late; switch to useEffect
options.why: Layout effects run synchronously before paint on the main thread; switching only adds a visible flicker.

options.text: It runs after every render and sets state, forcing extra synchronous renders and layouts
options.why: Each run reads layout and then sets state, so 500 rows force many synchronous layouts and re-renders before paint. Give the effect dependencies, or use a ResizeObserver.

options.text: offsetHeight is cached by React, so the rows see stale heights; read getBoundingClientRect instead
options.why: React caches nothing here, and both APIs force layout in the same way.

options.text: The ref is null during layout effects, so the code throws and React retries every row
options.why: Refs are attached before layout effects run.

explanation: With no dependency array the layout effect runs after every render, reads layout (forcing the browser to compute it) and sets state, which triggers another synchronous render before paint. Across 500 rows that is a lot of blocking work. Measure only when inputs change, batch measurements, prefer CSS where possible, or use a ResizeObserver to react to real size changes.

options.text: It doesn't debounce: each render creates a new debounced function with its own timer, so every keystroke still triggers a request
options.why: The timer state lives in the debounced function, which is recreated on every render.

options.text: A fix is to create the debounced function once (useMemo or useRef) and cancel it in an effect cleanup on unmount
options.why: One stable debouncer shares one timer across renders, and cleanup avoids calls after unmount.

options.text: It works correctly, because setQ is batched and so the component never re-renders while the user types
options.why: Every keystroke re-renders Search, which recreates the debouncer.

options.text: The fix is to wrap the whole onChange handler in useCallback, keeping the debounce call inside it as written
options.why: If the debouncer is still created during render, it is still a new one each time.

options.text: Debouncing state updates like setQ is required, otherwise the input loses characters
options.why: The input's own state should update immediately; only the expensive side effect should be debounced.

explanation: A debounced function keeps its timer in its closure. Creating it during render makes a fresh one per keystroke, each firing once 300 ms later, so nothing is coalesced. Create it once (`useMemo(() => debounce(fn, 300), [])` or a ref) and cancel it on unmount. Keep the input's value state urgent. Alternatively, `useDeferredValue` handles slow rendering without timers.

options.text: Total, because reduce inside render is never memoized by the compiler
options.why: Pure derived values like this are exactly what the compiler memoizes.

options.text: Sorted, because it mutates its `items` prop during render
options.why: Array.prototype.sort sorts in place, so the parent's array is modified.

options.text: Greeting, because the compiler cannot memoize property access on objects
options.why: Reading properties from props is fine; the compiler tracks those dependencies.

options.text: None of them; the compiler can safely optimise any valid JavaScript
options.why: The compiler assumes components are pure and props and state are immutable.

explanation: The React Compiler memoizes based on the assumption that components follow the Rules of React: pure render, no mutation of props or state, hooks rules. `items.sort()` mutates a prop in place, so cached results can go stale and the compiler (with its lint rules) flags or skips such code. Use `items.toSorted(...)` or copy first. Pure components such as Total and Greeting are ideal targets.
reference: react.dev: React Compiler; Rules of React

stem: Which two statements about the React Compiler (v1.0) are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: It automatically memoizes components, values and callbacks at build time, so most manual useMemo, useCallback and memo become unnecessary
options.why: That is its main purpose.

options.text: It can't make an update cheaper when the data really did change, such as a context value that changes on every keystroke
options.why: Memoization skips work for unchanged inputs; changed inputs still need rendering.

options.text: It deep-compares props at runtime, so new objects with equal contents no longer cause re-renders
options.why: It adds fine-grained caching of values, not runtime deep equality checks.

options.text: It removes the need for keys in lists, because it tracks list items by position automatically
options.why: Keys are part of reconciliation, which the compiler does not change.

options.text: It works correctly even with components that mutate state or props in place
options.why: Mutation breaks its assumptions; such code must be fixed or opted out.

explanation: The compiler transforms components to cache JSX, values and callbacks based on their dependencies, which in practice gives the effect of memo, useMemo and useCallback everywhere. It does not change React's semantics: when inputs really change, work still happens, and architectural problems (over-broad context, huge lists) still need design fixes. It requires code that follows the Rules of React.

options.text: 1: only Plain, because every other child is memoized
options.why: memo only helps when every prop is identical.

options.text: 2: Plain and MInline
options.why: MStyle and MKids also receive brand-new objects each render.

options.text: 4: Plain, MStyle, MKids and MInline
options.why: Plain is not memoized, and the other three each get a new object, element or function.

options.text: 6: memo makes no difference when the parent itself re-renders
options.why: M and MCb receive identical props and are skipped.

explanation: Plain is not memoized, so it always renders. M has no props, so it skips. MStyle gets a new object literal, MKids a new children element and MInline a new arrow function: all three fail the shallow check. MCb gets a stable `useCallback` reference and skips. Measured in React 19: Plain, MStyle, MKids and MInline each rendered once; M and MCb did not render.

options.text: Neither: the value object is the same reference and both components have unchanged props
options.why: useMemo keeps the same object while user is unchanged, so no consumer is notified.

options.text: Reader only, because context consumers always re-render when their provider's parent renders
options.why: Consumers re-render only when the value changes by Object.is.

options.text: Both, because the Provider element itself is new on every render
options.why: A new Provider element with the same value notifies no one.

options.text: Other only, because memo does not cover components rendered inside providers
options.why: memo works the same anywhere in the tree.

explanation: With `useMemo`, the provider value keeps the same identity while `user` is unchanged, so React does not notify consumers, and both memoized children skip because their props are unchanged. With the inline `{ user }` from the earlier question, Reader would re-render on every App update. Measured: 0 renders with the memoized value, 1 render of Reader with the inline value.
reference: react.dev: useContext (Optimizing re-renders when passing objects and functions)

options.text: Remove `selected` from the dependency array so the callback stays stable
options.why: That freezes `selected` at its first value inside the callback, so the comparison becomes wrong.

options.text: Stop reading `selected` in the callback so it needs no dependencies
options.why: Call `setSelected(id)` directly (or use the updater form); setters are stable, so the callback needs no dependencies and only the cells whose isSelected changed re-render.

options.text: Wrap `cells.map(...)` in useMemo with `[cells]` as its only dependency
options.why: The JSX depends on `selected` too; leaving it out shows stale selection state.

options.text: Replace useCallback with useMemo returning the same arrow function
options.why: useMemo with the same dependency changes identity just as often.

explanation: Because `select` depends on `selected`, it gets a new identity every time the selection changes, and that new prop invalidates every memoized Cell. Removing the read of `selected` (setters are stable, and the updater form can read the current value) keeps the callback stable, so only the cells whose `isSelected` flipped re-render. Measured: a callback whose dependency changes re-renders its memo child on every update.
reference: react.dev: useCallback (Updating state from a memoized callback)

stem: A chat log of 10,000 messages with very different heights is rendered with `react-window`'s `FixedSizeList` set to `itemSize={60}`. What goes wrong, and what is the right approach?

options.text: Nothing: the list measures each row automatically after mounting and corrects the layout
options.why: A fixed-size list positions every row at index × itemSize and never measures.

options.text: Rows overlap or leave gaps; use a variable-size or measuring virtualizer
options.why: A fixed-size list positions row i at i × 60 px, so variable content overlaps; use VariableSizeList, react-window v2 dynamic heights, or TanStack Virtual's measurement.

options.text: Every row renders at once, because virtualization is disabled when heights differ
options.why: It still renders only the visible window, just at wrong positions.

options.text: The browser's find-in-page and screen readers work exactly as before, so only scrolling is affected
options.why: Off-screen rows are not in the DOM, which affects find-in-page and assistive technology too.

explanation: Virtualized lists render only the rows in view and position them absolutely, so they must know each row's offset. A fixed-size list assumes every row has the same height. With variable content you need a variable-size list (`VariableSizeList` or react-window v2's dynamic row heights) or a measuring virtualizer such as TanStack Virtual. Remember the trade-offs: off-screen content isn't in the DOM for find-in-page or screen readers.
reference: react-window docs; web.dev: Virtualize long lists

stem: Put the arguments of the `<Profiler onRender>` callback in the order React passes them.

options.text: `id`
options.why: The id prop of the Profiler that committed.

options.text: `phase`
options.why: "mount", "update" or "nested-update".

options.text: `actualDuration`
options.why: Time spent rendering this commit.

options.text: `baseDuration`
options.why: Estimated time for the whole subtree without memoization.

options.text: `startTime`
options.why: When React began rendering this update.

options.text: `commitTime`
options.why: When React committed this update.

explanation: React 19 calls `onRender(id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime)`: six arguments (verified by logging the callback). `phase` tells you whether the tree mounted or updated; comparing `actualDuration` with `baseDuration` shows how much memoization saves. Profiling adds overhead, so it is off by default in production builds.

options.text: Nothing extra: React caches lazy components by the import path
options.why: React identifies lazy components by the object `lazy()` returns, not by path.

options.text: Chart remounts as a new type: it suspends, re-imports and loses state
options.why: Each call to lazy() returns a new component type, which React treats as a different component.

options.text: The chunk is downloaded once, but Chart keeps its state because its position in the tree is the same
options.why: Position only preserves state when the type is the same.

options.text: React throws an error because lazy can't be called during render
options.why: It doesn't throw; it simply misbehaves, which is why the docs warn about it.

explanation: Call `lazy` at module top level. Inside a component, every render creates a new lazy type: React unmounts the old subtree, the new one suspends and shows the fallback, the loader function runs again, and all state below resets. Measured with React 19: after a parent re-render, the import function ran a second time and the Suspense fallback reappeared.

stem: A root `AppContext` provides `{ theme, user, setUser }`. A profile form calls `setUser` on every keystroke, and the whole app (hundreds of consumers of `theme`) re-renders while typing. Which two changes help most? (Choose two.)

options.text: Split it into a ThemeContext and a UserContext so that theme consumers are not notified when the user changes
options.why: Each context notifies only its own consumers.

options.text: Keep the form's draft values in local state and update the shared user only on submit or blur
options.why: Fast-changing state should live in the smallest component that needs it.

options.text: Wrap the provider value in useMemo with `[theme, user]` as dependencies
options.why: user still changes on every keystroke, so the value changes every keystroke anyway.

options.text: Wrap every consumer of theme in React.memo
options.why: memo cannot block context updates.

options.text: Give the provider a key that changes on each keystroke so React remounts it cleanly
options.why: Remounting the provider remounts the entire app, which is far worse.

explanation: The root cause is that one context mixes slow-changing data (theme) with fast-changing data (a user being edited). Splitting contexts narrows who is notified, and moving draft state into the form keeps keystrokes local. Memoizing a value that legitimately changes on every keystroke does nothing, and memo doesn't apply to context.
reference: react.dev: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context

stem: A Web Worker computes a 50 MB `Float32Array` for a visualisation, and posting it back to the main thread causes a long freeze. What is the main improvement?

options.text: Convert the array to JSON before posting, because strings are faster to clone
options.why: JSON encoding and parsing 50 MB is slower than a structured clone of the binary data.

options.text: Post the underlying ArrayBuffer as a transferable, `postMessage(arr, [arr.buffer])`, so it is moved instead of copied
options.why: Transferring hands over ownership without copying, in constant time.

options.text: Wrap the setState that stores the result in startTransition so the copy happens in the background
options.why: The copy happens during message delivery, outside React, before your setState runs.

options.text: Use SharedArrayBuffer by default, since it needs no special server headers
options.why: SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation (COOP and COEP headers) to be available.

explanation: `postMessage` structured-clones data by default, which copies all 50 MB. Passing the buffer in the transfer list moves ownership to the receiver in constant time (the worker's array becomes detached). Moving heavy computation into workers keeps React renders and input responsive, but you must also avoid expensive copies when the results come back.

stem: After a real update has been rendered, a handler calls `setCount(c => c)` twice in two separate clicks, leaving the value unchanged each time. A `console.log` in the component body shows "render" once after the first of these clicks and not after the second. Why?

options.text: It is a Strict Mode artifact: in production neither click would log anything
options.why: This happens without Strict Mode as well; it is part of React's bail-out logic.

options.text: React sometimes has to call the component once to confirm the state is unchanged, then bails out without rendering children or committing
options.why: The eager bail-out only applies when no update is pending on either copy of the component; otherwise React checks during render.

options.text: The first click re-rendered the whole subtree, because React compares state only after the children render
options.why: Children were not re-rendered and nothing was committed.

options.text: Functional updaters always force one render; plain values never render when equal
options.why: Both forms bail out the same way; the difference comes from React's internal state, not the updater form.

explanation: When new state is `Object.is`-equal to the old, React tries to bail out before rendering. If it can't prove that cheaply (for example right after an update, when the alternate fiber still has work recorded), it renders the component itself, sees nothing changed, and skips its children and the commit. The docs note React "may still need to call your component before skipping the children". Measured in React 19: one parent render with zero child renders, then nothing on the next identical update.

options.text: Add a custom comparator that ignores `children`
options.why: Then Toolbar would never show new children, even when they really change.

options.text: Memoize the children element: `const items = useMemo(() => <><Logo /><Menu /></>, [])` and render `<Toolbar>{items}</Toolbar>`
options.why: The children prop keeps the same identity, so memo's comparison passes.

options.text: Wrap Logo and Menu in React.memo
options.why: That only affects whether Logo and Menu render; Toolbar still gets a new children prop.

options.text: Pass the children with spread syntax `{...[<Logo />, <Menu />]}`
options.why: Spread creates new elements and a new array each render.

explanation: JSX children are recreated on every render, so a memoized wrapper that takes children always misses. Memoizing the element tree makes `children` referentially stable: measured, the memoized wrapper rendered zero times on parent updates. Alternatively, restructure so the wrapper is rendered by a component that does not re-render, or let the React Compiler cache the JSX automatically.
